newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Philippines moves forward.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Philippines moves forward.

text.p: The Philippines made another move toward joining the Asian tigers on Monday with news that it would exchange Brady bonds for uncollateralized debt.

Finance Secretary Roberto de Ocampo announced that the government is offering two new uncollateralised bonds in exchange for US$1.9 billion worth of U.S. Treasury note-backed Brady bonds, otherwise known as par bonds.
Brady bonds, named after former U.S. Treasury Secretary Nicholas Brady, are bonds backed by the U.S. Treasury but with repayment made by a sovereign lesser developed country.
The Philippine Brady bonds will be exchanged for a new U.S. dollar fixed rate bond due 2016 and/or a U.S. dollar floating rate note issue due 2011.
The exchange offer will take the form of a modified Dutch auction. J.P. Morgan Securities is lead manager for the issue and Morgan Guaranty Trust is the exchange agent.
"Now it's just a question of waiting to see how many will take up this offer," said one syndicate manager in Hong Kong.

"But I think that the Philippine government has been buying back those issues quite a bit over the last few weeks or months, so the amount of bonds actually oustanding will be only a fraction of the total issue size," he added.
De Ocampo said the retirement of the par bonds was in line with the government's shift from high-yielding debt issues to commercial rated issues launched in international capital markets.
Economists have been bullish on the Philippines for some time due to its strong economic performance. Many have called the country the next Asian tiger.

A larger-than-expected 7.06 percent increase in gross national product in first-half 1996 has reinforced the positive outlook. The government's peace pact with Moslem rebels signed today after 24 years of fighting has further improved sentiment.

Philippines bank floating rate certificate of deposit issues have been popular with Asian bankers over the last several months, while corporate issues launched in the Eurobond market have found a receptive audience.

Metrobank currently is in the market with the first-ever five-year FRCD for a Philippines bank--most issues have been only three-years in tenor--and PCIBank has mandated Merrill Lynch to lead manage the first fixed-rate Eurobond for a Philippines bank.
The US$100 million five-year bond is expected to be priced at 125-135 basis points over comparable Treasuries.
In another development that could bring the Philippines into the global capital markets, ING Barings today said it has made proposals to arrange peso-denoniminated bonds in the international market.
The issuer could be any triple-A rated institution or any other multilateral institutions looking for alternative investment opportunities, ING Barings said.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell made a similar proposal recently.
Bankers said such an issue would appeal mostly to Philippine private investors, but could attract some international interest if the issuer is rated highly enough.

In other debt news, Korea Exchange Bank Hong Kong branch launched and closed a 364-day HK$500 million FRCD. The issue pays 30 basis points over the one-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate. Fees are 7.5 basis points.
Chase Manhattan Asia, Jardine Fleming and Sakura Finance Asia are the arrangers.
